title: Emergency-response multisigs are exempt from signer and threshold minimums because they cannot move assets
content:
A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.2.1 sets the baseline: "a minimum of three (3) signers" and "a signing threshold of at least fifty percent (50%) of total signers." A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.2.2.1 then carves out, "[a]s a transitionary measure," any multisig "whose sole capability is an emergency-response function — such as an emergency freeze, pause, or the removal of a compromised Relayer — that cannot move, custody, or allocate assets." Such a multisig "is not subject to the minimum signer or signing-threshold requirements" and "is configured to optimize for rapid emergency response."

The reasoning is capability-scoped rather than trust-scoped, which is the right form for a security exemption. Signature thresholds exist to make theft require collusion; where the key provably cannot take value, the threshold buys little and costs the seconds that determine whether a pause lands before an exploit completes. Requiring two of three signers to coordinate during a live attack is itself a risk.

The residual exposure is griefing, not theft. A single compromised key on a low-threshold pause multisig can halt the protocol, and denial of service against a stablecoin is a serious harm even with no funds lost. The provision accepts that trade explicitly by naming itself transitionary, "pending the development of specific threshold requirements for emergency-response Multisigs."

The general exception framework (A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.2.2) is tighter — Core GovOps may grant case-by-case relief with the Protocol Security Workstream Lead, and its examples require that "parameters are tightly bounded and set by governance" *and* that "a defined recovery or replacement mechanism exists in the event of Multisig failure or compromise." Bounded authority plus a recovery path is the pattern that substitutes for signer count.
description: A multisig whose sole capability is freeze, pause or Relayer removal is released from the 3-signer and 50% rules and configured for speed — the exemption rests on limited capability, not on trust.
